newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel clashes heighten economic uncertainty-UBS.
newsitem.headline: Israel clashes heighten economic uncertainty-UBS.

text.p: The recent violence increases the likelihood that the Israeli government will have little time to focus on the economy in the near term, which could result in currency turbulence, a UBS economist said on Tuesday.
Last week's bloody clashes between Palestinians and Israelis that killed 72 people were sparked by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's decision to open a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.

The events sparked volatility in Israel's currency markets, with the dollar on Monday reaching as high as 3.24 shekels against 3.17 shekels on Thursday. On Tuesday the dollar was trading at 3.19 shekels.

Union Bank of Switzerland senior economist David McWilliams said the chances are now greater that Israel will undergo what he calls the "risk case scenario" where the government fails to take significant economic action.
In this scenario, the shekel could fall to 3.5 shekels to the dollar by the end of 1996, he said.
"As long as Netanyahu is consumed by political problems, it is highly unlikely economic problems will be at the top of the agenda," McWilliams told Reuters.

Israel's economic problems, a result of expansive fiscal policy and erratic monetary policy, sparked a flight to liquidity in recent months with Israelis moving out of stock and bonds and into short-term deposits.

"Liquid assets account for 30.6 percent of Israel's savings portfolio of $168 billion against 22 percent in 1994. Equities now account for only 14 percent," McWilliams wrote in a report published on September 26.

"The move into the short-end has signalled a collective 'thumbs down' from the public to both policy credibility and by implication to the capital markets which are ultimately dependent on confidence in policy markets," the report said.

If the government fails to focus on the economy the increased uncertainty could spur a swing into dollars. "In the risk case, the forces which could amass against the shekel over the next few weeks may be largely negative," McWilliams said.
He estimates there is close to $40 billion in very liquid positions in Israel that potentially could move out of shekels, including a short dollar position of $11 billion.
The falling shekel may then force the government to act, bringing forward 4.9 billion shekels in spending cuts planned for 1997.
In this case, gross domestic product would grow by only 2.3 percent next year while the shekel could fall even further, to about 3.9 shekels to the dollar.
"Inflation may rise but possibly not by as much as the central bank maintains because we would have to take into account the economic slowdown," McWilliams said.
Inflation could reach 14 percent against an expected 12 percent this year, he forecast.
Ironically, this scenario would actually benefit several sectors of the stock market.

"For investors this is one of the best possible outcomes -- it blows froth off the Israeli market. There is decent beer at the bottom but too much froth on top. This will reveal some very dynanmic companies in the Israeli market," McWilliams said.
"Given the weaker shekel outlook exporters are at bargain basement prices waiting to be snapped up, as are several domestic plays unaffected by the economic slowdown."
